overview.text: Gioachino Rossini (1792–1868) was an Italian composer whose prolific career made him a leading figure in early nineteenth-century opera. Born in Pesaro to musical parents, he studied in Bologna and began his theatrical career in Venice. He wrote both comic operas, including The Barber of Seville and La Cenerentola, and serious works such as Tancredi and William Tell. After working in Italy, Rossini settled in Paris, where William Tell premiered in 1829 as his last opera. He later composed sacred and shorter works, but his best-known achievements remain his operas, notable for spanning comic, serious, and in-between forms.

key_facts.text: Rossini was born in Pesaro on February 29, 1792; his father played horn and trumpet, and his mother was a singer.
He studied music in Bologna and made his theatrical debut in Venice in 1810 with the comic opera La cambiale di matrimonio.
The Barber of Seville premiered in 1816 and La Cenerentola in 1817; both are among his celebrated comic operas.
Rossini also wrote serious opera, including Tancredi; his final opera, William Tell, premiered in Paris in 1829.
After stepping away from opera, he continued to compose other music, including the sacred Stabat Mater and shorter works.
